newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil mkts still confident re-election will pass.
newsitem.headline: Brazil mkts still confident re-election will pass.

text.p: Brazil's Congress will eventually pass a constitutional amendment allowing presidential re-election as lawmakers are unlikely to risk its overwhelming approval in a national plebiscite, market analysts said Wednesday.
"Negotiations will be tough, but I don't think Congress is going to want a plebiscite," said Luiz Fernando Figuereido of Banco BBA-Creditanstalt.

Market analysts said the PMDB party, the largest in Congress and a government ally, is likely to rethink its opposition to re-election because it has no strong candidate of its own for 1998 and would lose its link to power.
"It's better to stick with the devil you know, so I think they'll go to bed together," said one analyst, who requested anonymity. "At the end of the day, it's in everyone's interest to do that."
Despite fears political setbacks may force the measure to a plebiscite, analysts remain optimistic Congress will pass an amendment allowing President Fernando Henrique to stand for re-election.

They said maverick members of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) are unlikely to risk breaking with the government by blocking the measure in Congress only to have it overwhelmingly approved later in a popular vote.
Recent polls show 65 percent of Brazilians approve a re-election amendment while 35 percent oppose it, a sign Cardoso has strong public support on the issue, analysts said.

In a setback to opponents of re-election, a special congressional panel voted 19-11 Wednesday to approve the amendment. However, the government is unsure it has the three-fifths majority to put the amendment to a vote in the Lower House.
Perhaps as a sign of how far Cardoso has to go, Brazil's stock markets were unmoved by Wednesday's committee vote.
Until this week, Cardoso thought he had locked up the PMDB's votes. But in a blow to the government, the PMDB's rank-and-file voted in a one-day convention Sunday to oppose re-election.
Nonetheless, the government still has tough negotiating ahead before it will be able to seek house approval.
"In the end it's going to be approved by Congress, because a referendum would be bad for everyone, but it's going to be very difficult," said Robert Drummond of Bozano, Simonsen.

Analysts said the lower house is likely to cast an initial vote in late January and a second one in February after house and Senate leaders are elected early in the month. Senate approval may come in March, theysaid.
Meanwhile, a plebiscite would not possible before April, they added.
